analysis.one_liner: Makes large factory farms pay for disaster culls, protects their workers, and tightens humane slaughter rules.
analysis.headline: The Industrial Agriculture Accountability Act never received a committee vote or any floor action in the House before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new USDA office that large industrial livestock operators must register with, submit disaster plans to, and pay annual fees to. Operators would be liable for the full costs of disaster events and mass culls of animals, owe severance and health coverage to workers who handle the culls, and compensate neighbors for damage. It would also ban the most painful mass-killing methods, extend humane slaughter protections to poultry, end higher-speed slaughter and plant self-inspection programs, and fund more federal inspectors.
analysis.who_benefits: Slaughterhouse and processing workers, who would get 12 weeks' severance and two years of full-premium health coverage after disaster culls; contract growers, who would be owed roughly 180 days of lost revenue if their contracts are terminated after a disaster; neighbors of large feeding operations, who would be compensated for health and property damage; and taxpayers, who currently share the cost of depopulation events. Small and higher-welfare farmers would gain a grant program and expanded inspection access meant to level a highly concentrated market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Meatplant workers, contract growers, factory-farm neighbors

how_it_helps.text: Workers who perform or are affected by depopulation work would be owed 12 weeks of severance at their average weekly earnings if fired within 60 days of a disaster event, plus two years of a silver-level health plan with the full premium paid by the operator [S3].

Contract growers whose contracts are terminated after a disaster would be owed an amount equal to their revenue from the industrial operator over the preceding 180 days, and both workers and growers would get whistleblower protections and the right to sue with attorney's fees and double damages [S3].

Industrial operators would be liable for all costs of disaster events and depopulation, including disposal that meets environmental laws, plus compensation to neighboring residents for adverse health impacts and loss of property value and enjoyment [S3].

The bill bans sodium nitrite poisoning, ventilation shutdown, ventilation shutdown plus, and water-based foaming as mass-killing methods, with penalties of up to $1,000 per animal and 10-year loss of federal contracts and federal inspection eligibility [S3].

It terminates programs allowing slaughter speeds above existing limits or replacing federal inspectors with company employees, and authorizes roughly $60 million per year for additional OSHA inspectors and $50 million per year for more USDA meat and poultry inspectors [S3].
Poultry would be brought under the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act, which currently leaves about 98 percent of animals slaughtered for food outside federal humane slaughter protections [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large industrial livestock operators — those running 2,500-plus swine or 82,000-plus birds — would pay annual fees of at least $1 per animal unit, carry full disaster and depopulation liability, fund worker severance and health coverage, and compensate neighbors. Meatpackers would bear the cost of slower slaughter lines, federal inspection requirements, and a $750 million program to convert poultry plants to controlled-atmosphere stunning. Some costs would likely reach consumers through meat prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large industrial livestock operators and meatpackers

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be costly: annual registration and fees, disaster plans, full liability for culls and disposal, severance, and two years of paid premiums for cull workers all fall on operators, and an honest supporter would acknowledge some of this shows up in retail meat prices [S3].

The thresholds (2,500 swine, 82,000 birds) draw the line at large operations, but the fee floor and liability rules could still pressure mid-size producers near the cutoffs and favor operators large enough to absorb compliance costs [S3].

The bill appropriates $750 million for poultry plants to switch stunning methods and authorizes over $100 million a year in new inspector funding, new federal office and enforcement machinery, and a 10-year phase-in for poultry humane-slaughter coverage and the 8-hour transport limit — a slow and expensive regulatory build [S3].
Banning beta-agonist growth drugs like ractopamine and zilpaterol would remove a tool producers use for feed efficiency, raising production costs in an industry with thin margins [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: workers, growers, neighbors, animals, and taxpayers gain protections and cost-shifting they currently lack, while the price is borne by the large operators whose culls and labor practices created the problem, with some pass-through to meat prices. The design has rough edges — the slow phase-ins and the risk of squeezing mid-size producers near the thresholds — but the bill's costs fall mostly on the parties it regulates, funded largely by operator fees rather than general revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Education and Workforce committees and then to subcommittees, and never received a markup, committee vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James McGovern introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, joined by Reps. Blumenauer, Meng, Norton, Hayes, Krishamoorthi, and Khanna as original cosponsors [S3].
Fifteen Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored [S4].
The bill was referred to three committees — Agriculture, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Education and the Workforce — on the day it was introduced [S5].
It went to the Economic Development subcommittee of Transportation and Infrastructure on February 3, 2023, and to the Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry subcommittee of Agriculture on March 6, 2023 [S5].
No markup, committee vote, floor vote, or further action of any kind is recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large industrial livestock operators and meatpackers, who avoided the fees, full disaster liability, worker and grower protections, and the end of faster slaughter lines that the bill would have imposed.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were Democrats, and the House Agriculture Committee, which controlled the bill's fate, took no action on it.

industries.industry: Industrial livestock and poultry operators (large factory farms and integrators)
industries.note: The bill's core targets: annual fees of at least $1 per animal unit, registration and disaster plans, full liability for disaster and depopulation costs, worker severance and health coverage, and compensation to neighbors. Its interest in avoiding these costs runs against the workers, growers, and communities the bill protects.

Terminates higher-speed slaughter and self-inspection programs, requires more federal inspectors, extends humane slaughter rules to poultry, and funds a $750 million transition to controlled-atmosphere stunning.

Growers would be owed about 180 days of lost revenue if terminated after a disaster, plus whistleblower protections and a private right of action — protections they lack against the large firms they contract with.

industries.industry: Small and higher-welfare farmers and small processors
industries.note: The bill funds higher-welfare transport research, expands inspection and technical assistance for smaller processing facilities, and bars grant recipients from selling to packers with over 10 percent market share, aiming to level a market the bill calls highly monopolized.
